overview: Yolngu peoples maintain distinct clan identities in Arnhem Land. Country, law, food, ceremony and art remain connected, while institutions at Yirrkala carry knowledge through contemporary media.

items.text: Dhuwa and Yirritja are complementary moieties connecting people, places and other living beings. In Miwatj, art and ceremony express relationships to fresh and saltwater Country.
Seasonal food gathering draws on both land and sea, including yams, fruit, fish and shellfish. Traditional owners connect these practices with law and ceremony.
Artists framed the Yirrkala petitions with clan designs in ochre, charcoal and pipeclay. These designs expressed relationships to land alongside text in English and Yolngu Matha.

Yolngu presented bark petitions to the Australian Parliament in1963 in response to mining plans made without adequate consultation. They understood the documents as a diplomatic offering between equal powers.

The Mulka Project combines a recording studio, production house, learning centre and cultural archive under Yolngu law and elder leadership. It trains community members and returns audiovisual records to communities.
A bark petition formerly held privately was formally returned to Yolngu at Yirrkala in2023. Its return forms part of continuing cultural custody.
